w: Commissioned in the 18th century by the sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah, this mosque at the royal mechouar has hosted the king's own Friday sermon since the era of Moulay Yusef - a tradition that has outlasted half a dozen renovations and just as many monarchs since.
s: Where the king himself gives the Friday sermon
_facts: Commissioned by Alaouite sultan Mohammed ben Abdallah in the 18th century
Located at the mechouar of Al-Sayeed
The king gives the Friday/Eid khotbah here, a tradition since Moulay Yusef
Renovated under Muhammad IV, Yusef, Muhammad V, Hassan II, Muhammad VI

w: The king's official residence sits behind its own historic walls in Touarga, sealed off from the rest of the city and fronted by a mechouar - the parade-ground square where the Ahl Fas Mosque and a run of government buildings crowd in among the gardens. Still the working seat of the Moroccan monarchy.
s: The king's walled residence, gardens and all
_facts: Primary and official residence of the king of Morocco, in Rabat
Sits in the commune of Touarga, enclosed by historic walls
Fronted by a mechouar with gardens, the Ahl Fas Mosque, and official buildings

w: Raised in 1812 by the sultan whose name it carries, this is the second-largest mosque inside Rabat's Andalusian-walled medina - a 32-metre minaret over a traditional courtyard and hypostyle hall, tucked between Souika and Sidi Fateh streets near the old Bab Bouiba gate.
s: A sultan's mosque behind the Andalusian wall
_facts: Built in 1812 by Alawi sultan Moulay Slimane
Second-largest mosque in the medina north of the Andalusian wall
1000 square metres, minaret 32 metres high, near Bab Bouiba gate

w: One of Zaha Hadid's last designs, its curling concrete form borrowed from the Bou Regreg river's bends and the sweep of Arabic calligraphy. Ground broke in 2014; the finished building then sat unopened for years, inaugurated in 2024 and not fully open to the public until 2026.
s: Zaha Hadid's last theatre, a decade in the making
_facts: Designed by Zaha Hadid, among her last projects before her 2016 death
Construction started 2014, officially inaugurated Oct 2024, opened to public April 2026
Curving design inspired by the Bou Regreg river and Arabic calligraphy
1,800-seat interior theatre plus a 7,000-seat open-air amphitheatre

w: Also called the mosque of the cobblers, after the trade once clustered around Souk Sebbat outside its door - this is the largest Friday mosque inside Rabat's old Andalusian medina, standing where the street still runs down toward the Chellah gate.
s: The medina's biggest mosque, named for cobblers
_facts: Also known as el-Kharrazin Mosque, 'mosque of the cobblers'
Largest Friday mosque in the historic Andalusian medina of Rabat
Located at the intersection of Souk Sebbat and Rue Bab Chellah

w: One of the largest mosques in Morocco, rising over central Rabat. The records on it are thin - no founding story, no named architect on file - but the sheer scale of the place does most of the talking for it.
s: One of Morocco's biggest mosques, thinly documented
_facts: Large mosque in central Rabat
One of the largest mosques in Morocco

w: Some call it Sale's second-oldest mosque; others insist it is the oldest of all, predating even the Great Mosque, tracing its founding to 1075 under the Almoravid emir Yusuf ibn Tashfin. Either way it was lost for centuries, buried under soil and rubble, before being dug out, restored, then rebuilt again in the 1960s.
s: A mosque lost for centuries, dug out, rebuilt twice
_facts: Historic mosque in the medina of Sale
Some sources date its founding to 1075 CE under Almoravid emir Yusuf ibn Tashfin
Deteriorated and was buried, then uncovered and restored in the early 20th century
New mosque built over the remains in the 1960s

w: A stretch of fortification marking the medina's southern edge - the line where Rabat's old town gives way to the newer city. Thin on recorded detail, but still standing, and still the boundary it always was.
s: The wall that still marks the medina's edge
_facts: Wall delimiting the southern border of the medina of Rabat

w: A 19th-century fortress in the Ocean neighbourhood, repurposed since 2020 to house Morocco's national photography collection - coastal artillery walls now hung with prints instead of watching for ships.
s: A 19th-century fortress, now hung with photographs
_facts: Housed in the repurposed 19th-century Burj Kebir Fortress, Ocean neighbourhood
Initiated by the National Foundation of Museums of Morocco
Inaugurated on 14 January 2020
